doc.title: Chuck Findley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 6, 2023

title: Auditioning for Buddy Rich and old-school hiring
summary: Shew recommends him, the Basin Street East audition, Buddy's demand to play like Sweets Edison, and praise for hiring on playing not nepotism.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: wanted to see Bobby. And we were doing an R&B band, it was a wonderful R&B band and we were opening for him and we were rehearsing. And it was after they did their sound check and they took their break and we were rehearsing and he told Sal Nestico he says, “I want you to hear this kid.” So they didn’t leave, they went up and they sat all the way up in the very top of the venue to listen to me play. And Shew, Bobby and I, we’re like brothers, real brothers. And next thing you know I get a call to fly to New York to audition for Buddy’s band, because he was on Buddy’s band after he left Woody. And I went in to audition. They must have auditioned a dozen trumpet players and Buddy was a stickler as far as like getting somebody to play. It was a split lead and jazz charts which it’s hard to find somebody to play the split lead and jazz because that’s what Shew and I did. We split that book right up down the middle you know. He’d play lead on one, I’d play jazz. I’d play lead on one and he’d play jazz. It was beautiful. And so I went in to audition in New York, Basin Street East. And I sat and I played and I thought I did a great job. But you know I was 18. So Buddy calls me into his dressing room to sit down in his dressing room. And he’s there in a smoking jacket and he says to me, “Kid, you’ve got the gig.” I said, “Oh fantastic, Buddy, man, wonderful.” He said, “Except when you play your solos I want you to play like Sweets Edison.” And I said, “Well I can’t do that.” I said, “If you want to get Sweets Edison then you call Sweets Edison.” And then there was a pause and then he said, “Kid, you’ve got the gig.” Because I stood up to him, I said I can’t do that, you get him. So that was the old school. And the old school was give me a — I’ll say it again — give me a prick that can play. There wasn’t any nepotism like there is these days. These days it’s just, you know I mean you’d be in a section where the guys didn’t get along but they played great. That was what the deal was. And they always had great bands, great bands, you know it’s very hard to find bands like that these days. Gordon Goodwin’s band has a friendly band. They all get along great and there’s no nepotism there, they’re all great players. But I don’t know how many bands are like that these days around the world. I’m sure there are, I just — but they’re far and — you know there’s no many of them I would say. I wish there were.
